concept.name: Student's t-distribution
concept.definition: A symmetric, bell-shaped probability distribution with heavier tails than the normal, parameterized by the degrees of freedom nu. It is the exact sampling distribution of the standardized sample mean when the population standard deviation is estimated from a small sample, and it converges to the normal distribution as nu grows.
concept.intuition: It is the 'cautious normal': when you estimate spread from limited data, the extra uncertainty fattens the tails, so extreme values are more likely than the bell curve suggests.
concept.mechanics: With shape parameter nu (a positive integer in testing contexts), the t density resembles the normal but with tail weight decreasing as nu increases; nu = 1 gives the Cauchy distribution and nu > 30 is practically normal. Its variance nu/(nu-2) exists only for nu > 2, and kurtosis only for nu > 4.
concept.formula: f(x) = (1 + x^2/nu)^(-(nu+1)/2) / (B(0.5, 0.5*nu) * sqrt(nu)), where nu is the degrees-of-freedom parameter and B is the beta function; variance = nu/(nu-2) for nu > 2.
concept.failure_modes: Low degrees of freedom imply very heavy tails - the mean is undefined at nu = 1 and the variance at nu <= 2 - so low-nu t models can break variance-based risk metrics. As a model for returns it captures symmetric fat tails but not skewness or volatility clustering.
concept.misconceptions: The t distribution is not just a small-sample curiosity: in finance it is used deliberately as a fat-tailed return model. Nor does 't-distributed test statistic' require the raw data to be t-distributed - it arises from normal data with estimated variance.
concept.example: A 95% confidence interval for a mean from n = 20 observations uses the t critical value with 19 degrees of freedom (about 2.09) instead of the normal 1.96, widening the interval to account for the estimated standard deviation.
